query: For nanoparticles composed of five or more metals in equal or near-equal atomic ratios and initially crystallized as a solid solution, what governs whether structural and chemical stability is maintained across catalytic and thermoelectric operating ranges of 473–1923 K? Formulate one testable mechanistic hypothesis, specify a controlled comparison, predict observations relative to the initial baseline, define the conditions under which the prediction should hold, identify supporting evidence, and state a result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: The nanoparticles’ ability to maintain a single-phase solid solution across 473–1923 K is governed by the degree of lattice distortion induced by differences in atomic radii. This lattice strain raises the kinetic barrier for atomic diffusion and phase separation, so that when the atomic size mismatch is sufficiently high (yet within the range for forming a single phase), the high configurational entropy is better able to stabilize the structure under thermal stress.
generation.material_initial_state: Nanoparticles composed of five or more metals in near-equiatomic ratios that are initially crystallized as a simple, chemically disordered (single-phase) solid solution.
generation.intervention: Adjust the choice of constituent metals to increase the atomic size mismatch (hence lattice distortion) while still maintaining near-equimolar composition and a solid-solution phase. The intervention is realized by synthesizing a batch with intentionally larger differences in atomic radii compared to a control batch with more similar atomic sizes.
generation.conditions: Both the test and control nanoparticles are exposed to catalytic and thermoelectric operating conditions spanning 473–1923 K, with all other processing parameters and environmental factors (e.g., atmosphere, support, and synthesis route) held constant.
generation.structural_mediator: Lattice distortion that suppresses atomic diffusion by imposing local strain fields.
generation.mechanism: Enhanced lattice distortion due to larger atomic size differences increases the kinetic barrier for diffusion. This reduces the rate of atomic rearrangements that would otherwise lead to phase segregation or chemical inhomogeneity, allowing the high configurational entropy of the alloy to stabilize the solid solution despite the severe temperature cycles.
generation.predicted_outcome: Under the high-temperature catalytic/thermoelectric conditions, the nanoparticles with higher lattice distortion will retain their single-phase, chemically uniform structure more effectively than the control nanoparticles with lower atomic size mismatch. In other words, the test particles will show reduced evidence of phase separation or chemical segregation compared to the baseline.
generation.baseline: HEA nanoparticles composed of similar constituent metals (i.e. with lower atomic size mismatch) that might begin to display some phase separation or chemical inhomogeneity when exposed to the same thermal conditions.
generation.boundary: This explanation holds as long as the modification of atomic size differences does not exceed the limit where the enthalpic interactions force the formation of intermetallic compounds; the alloy must remain in a single-phase solid solution regime by design.
generation.uncertainty: The precise quantitative threshold (i.e. the critical level of atomic size mismatch) beyond which the enhanced lattice distortion no longer improves stability is uncertain, and interactions from enthalpic contributions may also influence the stability.

falsification_experiment.design: Synthesize two sets of HEA nanoparticles in near-equiatomic ratios: one set using metal combinations that result in a higher atomic size mismatch (increased lattice distortion) and a control set using metals with more similar atomic radii. Subject both sets to extended thermal cycles within 473–1923 K under catalytic/thermoelectric test conditions.
measurements: X-ray diffraction (XRD) to detect phase changes or emergence of secondary phases
Transmission electron microscopy (TEM) and energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (EDS) mapping to assess chemical homogeneity and structural integrity
Long-term catalytic/thermoelectric performance measurements as an indirect probe of structural stability
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the HEA nanoparticles with increased lattice distortion do not show improved retention of their single-phase solid-solution structure (or if they exhibit similar or worse phase segregation or chemical inhomogeneity) compared to the control nanoparticles under identical thermal cycling, then the hypothesis would be falsified.

In contrast to conventional alloy materials based on single principal elements, high-entropy alloys (HEAs) have recently received considerable attention in various fields because of their unique physical and chemical properties. In principle, HEAs are produced by alloying five or more metal elements in nearly equal proportions (recently extended to 5 to 35 at%) into solid solutions with a high mixing entropy rather than an intermetallic phase. The resulting synergistic effect endows HEAs with high mechanical strength, good thermal stability, and catalytic activity. In particularly, HEAs displayed appraisable catalytic performance in electrocatalytic water splitting, ammonia oxidation and decomposition, and CO2 reduction. Mechanistic studies suggest that the ligand effect and distortion effect of HEAs, which arise from tuning the composition and geometric properties of HEAs to a large degree, could significantly modify the electronic properties of active sites and consequently improve their catalytic performance. The inherent synergy effect of HEAs provides possibility to boost the catalytic activity by combining suitable metals.
